parole.testo: From German avancieren + -íroz (verb-forming suffx), from Austrian German avanschieren, from French avancer (“to advance”).
Borrowed from Austrian German balhe, from Yiddish בהלה (behole, “confusion, clamour”).

A partial calque of Austrian German Zippverschluß and English zip fastener (ultimately from the English trade name zipper, from the verb zip) and the Hungarian noun zár (“lock, fastener”) as the second element.
Borrowed from Austrian German Tschecherl (“bar”), from Yiddish.
Borrowed from Austrian German detto (“ditto”), from Italian detto, past participle of dire (“to say”).
Borrowed from Austrian German Dunst (“mist, vapour, steam, idea”).
Borrowed from Austrian German Esszeug (“cutlery”), from essen (“to eat”) + Zeug (“tool”).

parole.significato: frikadelle, rissole, meatball (flat, pan-fried meatballs of minced meat)
parole.testo: First attested in 1894. Borrowed from Austrian German Faschiertes (“minced meat”).
Borrowed from Austrian German Fiaker, from French fiacre, after Hôtel de Saint Fiacre in Paris, which let coaches for hire.

parole.significato: fox terrier (whether smooth fox terrier or wire fox terrier)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Foxl.
Borrowed from Austrian German Frigidaire, from French frigidaire (“icebox”). Originally a brand-name of an American refrigerator company.

Borrowed from Austrian German Gigerl (“dandy”), from gigerl (“rooster, cock”). Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.

parole.significato: match (small wooden stick specially treated with chemicals to produce flame upon contact with another chemical, from th…
parole.testo: From gyú (“shortened from gyújt (“to light, to spark”), used as an adjective”) + fa (“wood”). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries, as a calque of Austrian German Zündholz. First attested in 1840.
Borrowed from Austrian German Karfiol, from Italian cavolfiore (“cauliflower”), from cavolo (“cabbage”) + fiore (“flower”).

First attested in 1789. Borrowed from Austrian German Karnische (“curtain-rod”), from French corniche (“cornice”), from Italian cornice (“frame, cornice”), from Latin corōnis (“curved line, flourish in writing”), from Ancient Greek κορωνίς (korōnís, “curved object”).

parole.significato: potato (the edible starchy tuber of the plant species Solanum tuberosum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Grundbirne (literally “ground pear”), more specifically from Bavarian grumper, krumbeer, krumpir. First attested in 1768. Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.

parole.significato: missionary (a person who travels attempting to spread a religion or a creed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Missionar (“missionary”), from French missionnaire (“missionary”).

parole.significato: press (device used to apply pressure to an item)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Presse. First attested in 1557.
Borrowed from Austrian German Bussi.

parole.significato: basket, bucket (a wooden or wickerwork container carried on the back, often used to carry grapes in a vineyard)
parole.testo: From German, more specifically from Bavarian–Austrian German; compare German Bütte (“tub, vat, barrel”) and English butt (“cask”).

parole.significato: bye-bye (a farewell greeting, formerly used by women, now mainly by children, accompanied by a waving hand gesture)
parole.testo: From Austrian German ba, pa, pah.

parole.significato: band (a strip of material wrapped around things to hold them together)
parole.testo: From Austrian German Band. First attested in 1470.

parole.significato: currant (the fruit of various shrubs of the genus Ribes, white, black or red)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German, more specifically from Bavarian-Austrian. Compare Austrian German Ribisel. Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc. First attested in 1720.
Borrowed from Austrian German Schampon, from English shampoo, from Hindi चाँपो (cā̃po), imperative form of चाँपना (cā̃pnā, “to press, knead”).
Borrowed from Austrian German Charge (“load, military rank”), from French charge (“charge”), from charger (“to charge”), from Medieval Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”).

parole.significato: heel (a crust end-piece of a loaf of bread)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Scherzl. Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.
Borrowed from Austrian German Schnittling (“chives”).
Borrowed from Austrian German Spalett (“shutters”), from Italian spalletta (“parapet”), diminutive of spalla (“shoulder”).

Borrowed from Austrian German Stoppel (“stopple”), from German stopfen (“to stuff”). Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.

parole.significato: service (a set of dishes or utensils)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Servis, from French service, from Latin servitium, from servus.
Borrowed from Austrian German Tante, from French tante, from Old French ante (“aunt”), from Latin amita (“paternal aunt”).

parole.significato: train of transport, baggage train, wagon train
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Train⁽ᵈᵉ⁾, from French train, from French traîner, from Late Latin *tragīnāre, from Latin trahere.

parole.significato: frankfurter, hot dog, Vienna sausage, wiener
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Würstel, diminutive of German Wurst (“sausage”). Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.

parole.significato: grounds (the sediment at the bottom of a liquid, especially coffee)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Austrian German Satz (“set, movement, coffee grounds, sentence”), from setzen (“to set, sit down”).

parole.significato: sock (a knitted or woven covering for the foot)
parole.testo: First attested in 1906. Borrowed from Austrian German. Compare Austrian German Socken, Sockerl, and German Socke. Ultimately from Latin soccus. Suffixed with -i to resolve the word-final consonant cluster, compare cetli from Bavarian zettl or German Zettel (/⁠ˈt͡sɛtl̩⁠/) etc.
Borrowed from Austrian German Giraffe, from Italian giraffa, from Arabic زَرَافَة (zarāfa, “giraffe”).
